summary.text: At \(n=5\), direct evaluation gives \(a(5)=4\) and \(a(4)=3\), so the difference is \(1\); but \(5=\lfloor2\phi^2\rfloor\), for which the conjectured Beatty characterization says the difference must be \(0\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{\sqrt2}+\frac12\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Thus \(a(n)\) is the nearest integer to \(n/\sqrt2\). We will disprove the conjecture by showing that its asserted description of the zero positions in the difference sequence fails at \(n=5\). The part involving the zeta tail \(s(m)\) is therefore irrelevant: since the conjecture is a conjunction, failure of the difference assertion alone disproves the whole conjecture.

We first compute \(a(5)\). Recall that \(\lfloor x\rfloor=m\) exactly when
\[
m\le x<m+1.
\]
We claim
\[
4\le \frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac12<5.
\]
For the lower inequality, it is enough to prove
\[
\frac72\le \frac5{\sqrt2}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt2>0\), this is equivalent to \(7\sqrt2\le 10\), or equivalently to
\(\sqrt2\le 10/7\). Both sides are nonnegative, and this last inequality follows by squaring, because
\[
2\le \frac{100}{49}
\]
(or, after clearing denominators, \(98\le100\)).

For the upper inequality, it is enough to prove
\[
\frac5{\sqrt2}<\frac92.
\]
Again using \(\sqrt2>0\), this is equivalent to \(10<9\sqrt2\), or \(10/9<\sqrt2\). Both sides are positive, and squaring proves this because
\[
\frac{100}{81}<2
\]
(or \(100<162\)). Hence
\[
4\le \frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac12<5,
\]
so
\[
a(5)=4.
\]

Next we compute \(a(4)\). We claim
\[
3\le \frac4{\sqrt2}+\frac12<4.
\]
The lower inequality is equivalent to
\[
\frac52\le \frac4{\sqrt2}.
\]
Because \(\sqrt2>0\), this in turn is equivalent to \(5\sqrt2\le8\), or \(\sqrt2\le8/5\). Squaring is legitimate because both sides are nonnegative, and gives
\[
2\le \frac{64}{25},
\]
which is true since \(50\le64\).

Similarly, the upper inequality is equivalent to
\[
\frac4{\sqrt2}<\frac72.
\]
After multiplication by the positive number \(2\sqrt2\), this becomes \(8<7\sqrt2\), or \(8/7<\sqrt2\). Squaring proves it because
\[
\frac{64}{49}<2,
\]
which is the same as \(64<98\). We therefore have
\[
3\le \frac4{\sqrt2}+\frac12<4,
\]
and hence
\[
a(4)=3.
\]

It follows that the difference at \(n=5\) is
\[
a(5)-a(5-1)=a(5)-a(4)=4-3=1.
\]

We now show that \(5\) nevertheless belongs to the Beatty sequence which, according to the conjecture, consists exactly of positions where this difference is zero. That sequence is
\[
A_{001953}=\{\lfloor k\phi^2\rfloor:k\ge1\}.
\]
Take \(k=2\). From \(\phi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\), we obtain
\[
\phi^2
 =\frac{(1+\sqrt5)^2}{4}
 =\frac{1+2\sqrt5+5}{4}
 =\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2},
\]
so
\[
2\phi^2=3+\sqrt5.
\]
Since \(4\le5<9\), monotonicity of the square root on nonnegative numbers gives
\[
2\le\sqrt5<3.
\]
Adding \(3\) yields
\[
5\le3+\sqrt5<6.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\lfloor2\phi^2\rfloor=5.
\]
Because \(2\ge1\), this proves that
\[
5\in A_{001953}.
\]

The conjecture asserts, for every \(n\ge1\), the equivalence
\[
a(n)-a(n-1)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in A_{001953}.
\]
Applying its right-to-left implication at \(n=5\), the membership just proved would force
\[
a(5)-a(4)=0.
\]
But the direct calculation above gives
\[
a(5)-a(4)=1.
\]
This contradiction shows that the claimed difference-sequence characterization is false. Therefore the full conjunction in the conjecture—including the zeta-tail inequalities and both Beatty-sequence characterizations—is false.
